## Deep Research findings

The evidence still points to **rising demand**, chiefly near Bus_29, as the cause—not the change in generator output. At 20:00, Bus_29 was at **0.943 p.u.** against a **0.950 p.u.** limit. Demand at Bus_28 and Bus_29 rose by **1.18 MW**, accounting for **71.1%** of the voltage fall; demand elsewhere contributed **28.7%**. The cause remained consistent when compared with a more comfortable point and the same time the previous day. Generator output changes were ruled out as a significant cause.

**Warning and prevention:** Bus_29 came within 0.01 p.u. of its limit at **18:30**, just **15 minutes** before the episode began at 18:45. The undervoltage episode lasted through **20:45** (2.25 hours), with a worst value of **0.932 p.u. at 19:15**. Holding the tested Gen_bus7 voltage set-point increase (1.000 to 1.014 p.u.) did **not** prevent the episode and caused a new violation on line **Bus_5–Bus_7 [L9]**.

A separate time-varying redispatch plan over **18:30–20:45** passed AC power-flow checks at all **10 studied 15-minute points**. It adjusted active power from all five generators—Gen_bus1, Gen_bus4, Gen_bus7, Gen_bus10 and Gen_bus12—and kept the minimum voltage at **0.950 p.u.** and maximum loading at **90.0%**. That supports that the episode could be avoided in the modeled study. **Caveat:** the plan result flagged that it starts at 18:30, whereas the original diagnosis was at 20:00; these are different operating points, so the plan figures describe the whole window, not the 20:00 snapshot. Also, its checks are at sampled ticks and do not establish actual generator ramp capability.

**Recurrence:** The measurements week contained **12 Bus_29 undervoltage episodes**. Demand was identified as the main cause in all **10 episodes investigated**, contributing **70.6–71.6%** of the change—evidence of a recurring problem in this dataset.

**Not established:** The available steady-state studies do not determine Bus_29’s voltage-stability margin to collapse, the units’ real-time ramp feasibility, dynamic stability, or the customer/equipment cost of the event. Those require stability and dynamic studies, actual unit response limits, and impact/cost data. The grid data also cannot establish whether weather, calendar or operating schedules, or a particular customer caused the demand rise; that would require external weather, schedule, or customer-level metering and event records.

📋 Data source: measurements. Load reactive demand was inferred using the default **0.95 lagging power factor**.

**Reading check.** CONDUCTOR re-ran the studies under readings the question left open, and the conclusion changes: with loads at power factor 1.00 instead of 0.95 (the default), the investigation finds nothing outside its limits. Say which reading you meant.
